summary: Describes a method for saving bandwidth when many RTP streams, such as voice trunks, travel the same path between two endpoints. It combines existing compression, multiplexing and tunneling protocols. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Many phone calls going the same way can share one big envelope instead of each having its own, and the envelope's label can be squeezed. This memo explains how to do that.

subtitle: How to squeeze many parallel RTP voice streams into one compressed, multiplexed tunnel to save bandwidth.

tldr.problem: Voice trunks carry many RTP streams in parallel over expensive long-distance links, and every stream pays for its own IP, UDP and RTP headers.
tldr.mechanism: TCRTP combines three existing protocols: Enhanced CRTP compresses the headers, PPP Multiplexing packs many payloads into one frame, and L2TP tunnels that frame end to end.
tldr.outcome: Savings depend on having enough simultaneous streams. For 5 G.729 calls the RFC's example shows 62 kbps with TCRTP over PPP against 124 kbps for normal VoIP over PPP. Video gains are insignificant.

today: RFC 4170 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 110). It has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 3545, RFC 3153 and RFC 3931.

sections.title: Why Save Bandwidth on Voice Trunks
sections.content:
TCRTP (Tunneling Multiplexed Compressed RTP) is a way to combine existing protocols for compression, multiplexing and tunneling to save bandwidth for some RTP applications, mainly Voice over IP (VoIP) in voice trunking.

Bandwidth cost is well known on customer access links, where classical CRTP (Compressed RTP) already helps. The RFC points out that the cost of long-distance WAN links is less acknowledged. Voice over ATM and Voice over MPLS save bandwidth because they have no IP, UDP and RTP headers, but they give up direct access to the voice-over-packet services available to Voice over IP.

The document is mostly about VoIP over high-delay networks, though the same combination can be used for other RTP applications such as video.
sections.eli5: Phone calls over the internet carry a lot of label text for very little talking. When lots of calls take the same long road, shrinking the labels saves real money.

sections.title: Where TCRTP Runs
sections.content:
The RFC describes two models. In the simplest, TCRTP is implemented in the voice gateways that terminate the RTP streams, and the gateways talk TCRTP over IP to each other.

In the second, an external concentrator sits at strategic places in the network. It creates and destroys TCRTP sessions dynamically, without any help from the RTP-generating endpoints. The gateways speak plain RTP over IP to the concentrator, and the concentrators speak TCRTP to each other.

This design also lets classical CRTP be used on links that have only a few active flows, where TCRTP is not efficient.
sections.eli5: Either the phone gateways pack the calls themselves, or a helper box in the middle collects calls from many gateways and packs them for the long trip.

sections.title: The Three Building Blocks
sections.content:
Header compression: ECRTP. CRTP works link by link, so compressing across several hops means doing the work twice on every router. It also assumes low delay and low loss, which a multi-hop path cannot promise, and packets can arrive out of order. TCRTP therefore uses Enhanced CRTP (ECRTP), which supports high delay, packet loss and misordering. Compression then runs end to end and saves bandwidth on all intermediate links.

ECRTP sends short deltas together with the full value when it updates context variables, and repeats the updates in N packets. When the compressor sees an unpredicted change in the RTP header it should send a COMPRESSED_UDP packet to resynchronize the decompressor. The sender's IP stack should transmit UDP checksums; if it does not, the compressor should use the CRTP Headers checksum.

Multiplexing: PPP Multiplexing. A tunnel adds its own IP and tunnel headers. Combining several RTP payloads in one multiplexed PPP frame amortizes that overhead over many payloads. Only LCP and IPCP (for header compression) are needed when the PPP link is set up: no IP address negotiation and no authentication.

Tunneling: L2TP. L2TP tunnels carry the ECRTP payloads end to end, and also carry the PPP setup messages such as NCP, so IPCP can negotiate the compression parameters.
sections.eli5: There are three tricks. Shrink each label, put many letters in one envelope, and send the envelope through a private pipe from one end to the other.

sections.title: Multiplexer Timing and Limits
sections.content:
A physical link's clock normally decides when a PPP multiplex frame is sent. A tunnel interface has no well-known transmission rate, so the RFC changes the transmitter logic. It should collect incoming payloads until either a specific number of octets, MAX-SF-LEN, has arrived, or a timer called T expires. Then the multiplexed payload is sent.

MAX-SF-LEN keeps the payload within the MTU of any physical link the tunnel might use. It should be less than or equal to the minimum of MRU-2 and 16,383 (14 bits). Timer T bounds the delay, is reset whenever a multiplexed payload is sent, and each transmitter should have its own. For voice, T would typically be 5-10 milliseconds.

Multiplexing only pays off with many streams. Loss of one multiplexed packet loses every flow inside it, and TCRTP is mostly useful when many RTP sessions run between a pair of endpoints. Also, if the tunnel carries EF-marked traffic, the tunnel header must carry the same EF marking, and EF and non-EF traffic should not be mixed in one EF-marked multiplexed tunnel.
sections.eli5: The packer waits until the envelope is full or a short timer rings, whichever comes first, so nobody's words wait too long.

sections.title: Encapsulation Format
sections.content:
The packet is built by concatenating the formats of the three protocols. An outer IP header (20 octets) comes first, then the multiplex PPP protocol field (1 octet), then for each payload a length field of 1-2 octets, a PPP protocol field (0-2 octets), and the ECRTP-compressed packet. That compressed packet holds a context ID (1-2 octets), a link sequence field (1 octet), the UDP checksum (0-2 octets) and then the RTP data.

When the tunnel carries multiplexed traffic, several PPPMux payloads travel in one IP packet.
sections.eli5: The big envelope has one outer address, and inside it each letter has a tiny label saying how long it is and what kind it is.

sections.title: Bandwidth Efficiency
sections.content:
Gain depends on multiplexing (more payloads per frame is better), the packet loss rate, and how fast IP and RTP header fields change. When loss is low (less than perhaps 5%), the robust operation of ECRTP with a parameter N is sufficient. N=1 protects against losing one packet, N=2 against two in a row, and higher values cost more bandwidth. Above about 5% loss, more advanced techniques are needed and are out of scope.

The RFC gives a formula for per-flow bandwidth. Its per-payload overhead of ECRTP and PPP mux is 6 octets, and the per-packet tunnel overhead is 25 octets (20 for IP, 4 for L2TPv3, 1 for the multiplexed PPP protocol ID). In the voice example (G.729, 20 ms packetization, 3 multiplexed payloads, random IPID) a call uses 16.4 kbits/sec against 12.4 for classical CRTP on one HDLC link. With a fixed IPID step, 13.8 against 11.2.

Over ATM, multiplexing fills cell padding that AAL5 would waste. On other networks the benefit is closer to link-by-link CRTP: with HDLC as layer 2, 7 flows must be multiplexed to break even. For MPEG-2 video the savings are insignificant (3.8 against 3.9 Mbits/sec), because headers are tiny compared to the payload.
sections.eli5: Packing many calls in one envelope helps a lot when there are many calls and the envelope would otherwise be mostly empty. With only a few calls, or with giant video chunks, it barely helps.

sections.title: Example Implementation and Negotiation
sections.content:
The example implementation creates an L2TP tunnel interface to a destination host. Routing sends RTP packets to that interface, where headers are compressed (ECRTP), payloads multiplexed (PPPMUX) and the result is carried over PPP and L2TP. The destination UDP port could distinguish RTP from non-RTP packets. The receiver does the same in reverse.

PPP setup uses LCP with no options, then IPCP with the IP-Compression-Protocol option using protocol 0x61. L2TP then sets up the tunnel with SCCRQ, SCCRP and SCCCN, and the session with ICRQ, ICRP and ICCN. Teardown uses StopCCN.
sections.eli5: The two ends first agree on the rules for the pipe, then open the pipe, and only then start sending calls through it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Attacks on TCRTP can target RTP headers and payloads, compressed headers, the multiplexing layer, or the tunnel negotiation and transport. Each component RFC covers its own issues, but combining them adds risks. Addressing information is more condensed, so there may be more risk of one stream's packets being delivered to another, especially over link layers that deliver packets with bit errors when the tunnel transport does not checksum all of the payload.

Addressing must stay unencrypted for compression and multiplexing to work, which may increase the opportunity for malicious misdirection. Basic RTP encryption covers the headers too and so is unsuitable, but a profile such as SRTP that encrypts only the payload works with header compression. Appropriate cryptographic protection should be incorporated into all TCRTP applications.
sections.eli5: Because the labels are small and must stay readable, a mixed-up letter is easier to deliver to the wrong person. Locking the contents of each letter is the best protection.
